title: Kikkoman: One Drop Out—Why Does It Matter Where Air Gets In? | Brand Stories
description:
From the refillable 150mL glass tabletop bottle of 1961 to the 200mL sealed bottle with an inner pouch of 2011, we also examine the tests of a 500mL soft-film prototype left at rest and subjected to drops in publicly available documents. Then we look at squeezing force near the end of a current 450mL PET bottle, closing its cap, and the storage tradeoff after breaking the seal. The prototype tests are kept separate from the marketed bottle models; the prototype is not presented as the production model's history. The designer's own recollections, original company announcements, museum labels, later original patents, and complete official FAQs distinguish different eras and bottle models. The later valve patent is not treated as the original design of the earlier glass bottle. Generic illustrations are conceptual diagrams, not cross-sections of every production model.

thumbnail.headline: No Air in the Wrong Place!

chapters.c08r1-01-01: After Pouring, Your Hand Still Has Work to Do
chapters.c08r1-02-08: The Big Bottle Gives Up Its Place at the Table
chapters.c08r1-03-01: A Clean Cutoff, but the Bottle Still Needs to Open
chapters.c08r1-04-06: The Freshness Pouch Meets the Letting-Go Problem
chapters.c08r1-06-04: The Last Little Bit Changes How You Store It

c8r10101.text: You only want to add one drop of soy sauce, but first you have to lift a big 1.8-liter bottle.

c8r10102.text: Kenji Ekuan recalled that when he received the commission in 1958, many households kept their large soy sauce bottles under the sink.

c8r10204.text: Before the small glass bottle arrived, you poured soy sauce from the big bottle into a small ceramic pot, then brought it to the table.

c8r10104.text: Will that little brown drop at the tip of the spout stay put?

c8r10105.text: But later, even the air entering the bottle became a problem.

c8r10106.text: When the last little bit won't pour out, the cap itself still gives you a choice.

c8r10107.text: I want to follow this drop of Kikkoman soy sauce through more than sixty years of changes to the bottle.

c8r10108.text: What does the bottle in your hand need to let out, so it can keep in what you want to preserve?

c8r10208.text: Kikkoman later explained that the aim was a small container you could put straight on the table after buying it.

c8r10209.text: It had to do more than hold soy sauce. Like cups and plates, it had to become something you used at mealtimes.

c8r10210.text: What should a retail bottle look like if it is going to sit beside the tableware?

c8r10212.text: The brief was wide open: how could soy sauce, which had been around for hundreds of years, be given a new look?

c8r10213.text: He said he had considered something like a faucet: turn it on, and soy sauce would flow out.

c8r10214.text: He had even considered changing soy sauce's black color. These were ideas, but what should finally go into the user's hands?

c8r10215.text: In the end, though, users still needed a bottle they could pick up, pour from, and put back on the table.

c8r10216.text: I want to know: when you pick it up, where do you grip it? And when you put it down, what keeps it standing?

c8r10217.text: Ekuan said he made the neck narrow, with a body that gradually grew wider and steadier toward the bottom.

c8r10218.text: He pictured fingers holding the neck, with the lines of the hand looking graceful too.

c8r10219.text: That was the designer's intention for the grip. It doesn't mean everyone's hand would take the same position.

c8r10220.text: In 1961, the company launched a 150-milliliter glass tabletop bottle.

c8r10221.text: The clear body also let you see how much soy sauce was left, without opening the cap and guessing.

c8r10223.text: It stands on the table, and your hand has found a place to grip. But when you pull your hand back, what happens at the spout?

c8r10301.text: When Ekuan recalled this problem, he began by comparing it with a teapot's spout.

c8r10302.text: He said that if the lower lip stuck out, as on a teapot, soy sauce would still drip down.

c8r10303.text: So he reversed the relationship between the two lips, making the upper one stick out farther.

c8r10304.text: That drop you worried about when pulling your hand back at the start comes down to this tiny tip.

c8r10305.text: This is my favorite part: the change looks small, but it shapes how you pull your hand back every time you finish pouring.

c8r10306.text: But is stopping drips all a spout needs to do?

c8r10307.text: A later exhibition label at New York's Museum of Modern Art said he had made nearly a hundred models.

c8r10308.text: The museum described two challenges: preventing drips and controlling the flow.

c8r10309.text: Ekuan himself recalled spending three years on the design before bringing its appearance and use together.

c8r10310.text: The label links the tip's inward slope with less soy sauce collecting at the end of the spout.

c8r10312.text: But with a spout this small, where do you put more soy sauce in when the bottle is empty?

c8r10313.text: You don't refill it through the spout. Remove the entire red cap, and the refill opening appears.

c8r10314.text: A GK publication says this opening is even slightly wider than the mouth of the big bottle from the start, making refilling easier.

c8r10315.text: When you pour onto a plate, you want a small outlet with a clean cutoff; when you refill the bottle, your hand needs a wider opening.

c8r10316.text: And when you lift that same cap to refill the bottle, where does your hand touch it?

c8r10317.text: A fiscal 2007 report from the European subsidiary KFE also records a change to the cap.

c8r10318.text: The raised parts on the cap were given rounded corners, to avoid hurting hands when opening it and refilling the bottle.

c8r10321.text: But does a clear bottle mean what's inside can always stay just as it was when first opened?

c8r10406.text: That makes me wonder: if you want soy sauce to get out and air to stay out, how does the original bottle need to change?

c8r10408.text: In 2010, Kikkoman first launched a sealed flexible pouch holding 500 milliliters.

c8r10401.text: You pick up this unpasteurized soy sauce, pour some, and put it back on the table. What's left has to wait until next time.

c8r10402.text: Kikkoman product developer Onda  later explained that this soy sauce skips heat pasteurization and uses special filtration to remove microorganisms instead.

c8r10403.text: But its color and aroma still change when it comes into contact with air.

c8r10407.text: According to the 2011 announcement, Kikkoman had already spent more than ten years researching sealed containers.

c8r10409.text: But once there is less soy sauce inside, can you still let go of that flexible pouch with confidence?

c8r10410.text: Onda later recalled that a nearly empty pouch struggled to stand on its own, and some people wanted to open the cap with one hand.

c8r10411.text: Imagine you're cooking, with one hand still holding something, while the other needs to let go of the pouch.

c8r10412.text: If you have to keep holding it up, you're losing more than just a little weight.

c8r10413.text: Could the outside stand on its own while the inside kept air away from the soy sauce?

c8r10414.text: The company turned to developing a bottle with a container manufacturer, going back and forth. Onda said this phase reached the market in ten months.

c8r10415.text: An announcement in July 2011 said the new 200-milliliter bottle would launch on August 10.

c8r10416.text: The first version took its shape from the old red-capped tabletop bottle, but what you held was a new bottle you could squeeze.

c8r10417.text: And how would the cap respond to that hand you can't spare while cooking?

c8r10418.text: The company listed a cap that opens with one push as a feature of this new bottle.

c8r10419.text: It also listed control of the amount dispensed by squeezing as a feature of this new bottle.

c8r10420.text: That year's new bottle was also said to keep soy sauce fresh for ninety days at room temperature after opening, a feature claimed by the company.

c8r10422.text: But when you relax your hand, the bottle still has to recover its shape so you can keep using it.

c8r10423.text: Where exactly should the air go, so it doesn't undo the work of keeping the soy sauce fresh?

c8r10501.text: This generation of bottle had an inner pouch for the soy sauce, placed inside an outer bottle.

c8r10502.text: As soy sauce pours out, the inner pouch shrinks as its contents decrease.

c8r10503.text: The announcement says that for the amount of soy sauce that leaves, a corresponding amount of air enters the space between the outer bottle and the inner pouch.

c8r10506.text: So how does the cap distinguish between liquid that needs to go out and air that needs to come back in?

c8r10507.text: The announcement describes a cap with two check valves, letting soy sauce through while keeping air out of the soy sauce pouch.

c8r10508.text: What I want to see even more is this: once you have let go, where does that little bit left in the spout go?

c8r10509.text: Later official educational materials linked this sealed tabletop bottle to a Japanese patent.

c8r10510.text: Granted in 2015, the original document describes a particular container and liquid-valve structure.

c8r10512.text: The document addresses liquid that does not return to the inner container, but remains near the outlet and could leak.

c8r10513.text: If you only close the route to the inner pouch, will the liquid left in the spout disappear by itself?

c8r10514.text: In this design, when you squeeze, pressure inside pushes an elastic liquid valve.

c8r10515.text: The valve moves along the passage, opening a route for the contents to flow through.

c8r10516.text: A separate part limits how far the valve can move.

c8r10517.text: When you let go, the pressure drops and the valve starts returning inward.

c8r10518.text: First it closes the connecting hole, then keeps moving back, enlarging a space inside the cap.

c8r10519.text: How can that small movement affect the tip of the spout?

c8r10520.text: The document says the expanding space can draw liquid left at the tip into the cap, a location separate from the inner pouch holding the soy sauce.

c8r10522.text: Outside air can now be drawn into the discharge opening.

c8r10523.text: The patent also includes an air valve and an outer air-intake passage in the structure, giving the incoming air and the liquid valve their own jobs.

c8r10524.text: And when you aren't squeezing the bottle and the outer cap is closed, does the liquid valve still need to be controlled?

c8r10525.text: The document also describes a structure with an outer cap. A sealing part inside that cap also helps restrain the liquid valve's elastic movement.

c8r6p01.text: But when you pick the container up again a few days later, does keeping air out mean it will still pour?

c8r6p02.text: In another publicly available patent, the applicant recorded the making and testing of a 500-milliliter soft-film prototype.

c8r6p03.text: They first molded a small rubber flap and its body as one piece, then applied pressure from inside and cut along the curved section.

c8r6p04.text: The short straight section was left uncut, forming a hinge for the flap.

c8r6p05.text: But if it takes an impact, will this little door just swing outward, or will the whole flap be pushed inside?

c8r6p06.text: The document first notes that an impact could force the flap into the tube, affecting both the check-valve function and liquid flow.

c8r6p07.text: It adds a raised feature on the side of the flap, which catches against the opening's edge to help stop it being pushed inward.

c8r6p08.text: The finished valve goes into the soft-film container, which is then filled with soy sauce. Next comes the wait until it is used again.

c8r6p09.text: After it has stood at room temperature for different lengths of time, will both things you want still hold true?

c8r6p10.text: Five samples were used for each time condition. First, they checked visually for air entering the container.

c8r6p11.text: Then they tilted the container to about forty-five degrees, to see whether the soy sauce flowed out smoothly.

c8r6p12.text: At all the observation points in the first two days, no air entry was seen and the flow was good. What about five days?

c8r6p13.text: After 120 hours, there was still no observed air entry; but when the container was tilted, soy sauce no longer flowed out naturally.

c8r6p14.text: The document records a small amount of soy sauce solidifying where the valve flap touched the edge of the opening.

c8r6p15.text: And if the container falls without soy sauce leaking outside, does that mean the flap is still in place?

c8r6p16.text: In a separate set of drop tests, samples without the outer cap were allowed to fall freely once, bottom first.

c8r6p17.text: With the outer cap fitted, the procedure changed to one drop bottom first, then one drop side first.

c8r6p18.text: Five samples were used for each condition. After the drops, they again checked air entry and liquid flow.

c8r6p19.text: In the group listed at 140 centimeters, both observations were still normal. What if it fell from higher up?

c8r6p20.text: In the 160-centimeter group, the flap was pushed into the tube, air entered, and soy sauce could no longer be poured out naturally.

c8r6p21.text: Yet in all the tests up to and including that height, the document reports no observed leakage of the contents to the outside.

c8r10527.text: Returning to bottles sold on the market, in 2018, the company changed the main material from PE to PET in a new 450-milliliter bottle.

c8r10526.text: When you pick up the clear sealed bottle, can you spot the inner pouch at a glance?

c8r10604.text: The difference between the two layers becomes easier to see once about half the bottle has been used.

c8r10606.text: If you can see a layer of gas even inside the pouch, has air leaked in from outside again?

c8r10607.text: Another current FAQ explains that nitrogen is also sealed inside the inner pouch to help push the soy sauce out.

c8r10608.text: The company says the nitrogen in the inner pouch does not oxidize the soy sauce.

c8r10609.text: The FAQ also says that when the bottle is tilted, moving nitrogen may cause a slight vibration that you can feel in your hand.

c8r10610.text: But with the same hand, why does it start to feel harder to squeeze as you use more of it?

c8r10611.text: Another FAQ says that as the pouch gets smaller, your hand's force increasingly presses it indirectly, through the air between the layers.

c8r10612.text: The way force is transmitted changes, so the company tells users to adjust how hard they press according to how much is left.

c8r10614.text: Once you let go, can you press the cap shut right away?

c8r10615.text: The official instructions for this current bottle say to leave it upright for a few seconds after use, then close the cap.

c8r10616.text: That makes it easier for soy sauce in the spout to return to the bottle, reducing the amount squeezed out when the cap closes.

c8r6u01.text: If you let go but the bottle stays dented, is the force of your hand the only issue?

c8r6u02.text: If soy sauce around the spout solidifies and blocks the air valve, the bottle may stay dented instead of springing back.

c8r6u03.text: The company says refrigerated bottles may also spurt as soon as the cap opens, or bubble over; other factors can cause these situations too.

c8r6u04.text: For a dirty spout, the manufacturer says to wet a soft cloth, wring it out firmly, and then wipe the spout.

c8r10618.text: With the seal working normally, the freshness guideline for this current bottle is 120 days at room temperature after opening.

c8r10619.text: There are exceptions for some products.

c8r10620.text: I also want to know: when that last bit you want is still inside, is there another way to get it out?

c8r10621.text: When very little is left, you can remove the entire cap by turning it to the right as seen from above, and get the remainder out.

c8r10623.text: But that also breaks the seal. Once the cap is removed, the official instructions require refrigeration instead.

c8r10630.text: That drop you wanted to keep at the start is ultimately tied to which opening the bottle lets you open, and which boundary you then need to protect again.

c8r10631.text: What would you do: break the seal to get the last bit out and move it to the fridge, or leave it there? Tell me in the comments.

c8r10632.text: Subscribe to Brand Stories. We'll keep looking at how everyday objects put invisible tradeoffs into your every move.
